title: Will AI Concerns Become a New Source of Terrorism?
gist: CSIS brief finds terrorism motivated by AI opposition is rare (two attacks in April 2026, neither fatal) and overwhelmingly peaceful opposition prevails, but outlines the conditions (copycat dynamics, extremist co-option, belief that politics has failed) that would raise the threat to AI executives, officials and facilities.

insights.claim: Only two attacks motivated by AI opposition qualify as terrorism: the April 6, 2026 shooting at the Indianapolis home of Councilor Ron Gibson, who backed a $500 million data center, and the April 10 Molotov attack on Sam Altman's San Francisco home and OpenAI headquarters; neither killed anyone and no organization is tied to either.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The base rate is low but the targets are named AI figures and local project supporters.

insights.claim: Vandals had destroyed more than 240 Flock Safety AI-powered license-plate cameras across the US by early September 2026.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Property attacks on AI-enabled surveillance are a measurable, ongoing pattern.

insights.claim: Daniel Moreno-Gama, charged in the Altman attack, carried a document calling for killing AI company CEOs and investors and listing names and addresses.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Executive-protection risk is specific and ideologically driven, not just site-based.

insights.claim: Plots against AI infrastructure so far were not clearly AI-motivated: Seth Aaron Pendley's 2021 plan to bomb AWS data centers was anti-government, and Ethan Early's abandoned 2025 thermite plot against xAI's Memphis data center stemmed from anger at Musk and Trump.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Data centers attract attackers with varied grievances, so the threat is broader than anti-AI ideology.

insights.claim: People associated with AI, such as executives, employees, local officials and project supporters, may be easier targets than hardened data centers and corporate offices with controlled access.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Security spend may shift toward personal protection and local-permitting stakeholders.

insights.claim: Existing extremist movements are already co-opting data center grievances, with white supremacist groups displaying antisemitic anti-data-center banners in Michigan and Texas in 2026, while jihadist groups have not adopted the cause.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Co-option widens the pool of potential perpetrators and the reputational risk of local opposition.

insights.claim: AI is a general-purpose technology so grievances fragment across uses (autonomous weapons, data centers, unemployment, surveillance), producing many small constituencies rather than one unified movement.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Diffuse grievances make organized campaigns less likely but harder to predict.

insights.claim: Terrorism becomes more likely when supporters conclude peaceful politics cannot achieve their goals; the key indicator is not how many people worry about AI but whether any part of the opposition regards violence as legitimate and necessary.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch rhetoric that elections and protest cannot stop AI development.
insights.quote: A key indicator is not how many people have concerns about AI, but whether any part of that broader opposition begins to regard violence as legitimate and necessary.

insights.claim: Opposition to disruptive technology has historically been mostly nonviolent and, when violent, more often targeted property than people (Luddites, anti-nuclear movements), with the Unabomber a rare exception.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Argues against over-inflating the threat from growing peaceful opposition.

insights.claim: Over 80 percent of Americans think AI development is moving too quickly, and opposition to data centers has become an electoral issue in several 2026 midterm campaigns, with both parties incorporating AI concerns that give opponents a nonviolent outlet.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Data-center siting is a live political and permitting risk for AI buildout.
